title: Recent developments in using digital technology in mathematics education
extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of selected recent developments in digital technology in mathematics education over roughly the previous five years. It addresses the broad question of how digital technologies are reshaping mathematics teaching, learning, assessment, classroom organization, and theoretical understandings of knowledge production in the field.

The review covers several adjacent topics rather than a single intervention: STEAM and critical making, redefined learning spaces, computer algebra systems and dynamic geometry, online collaboration through learning environments and social media, artificial intelligence and hyper-personalisation, multimodality including videos/AR/VR, the effects of COVID-19, and the epistemology of humans-with-media. The paper does not report a primary empirical sample; instead, it synthesizes literature and examples from mathematics education research, including work relevant to online, blended, and technology-rich environments.

The authors conclude that digital technology is shifting mathematics education away from routine calculation toward mathematical thinking, collaboration, and more individualized learning pathways. At the same time, they stress important tradeoffs and risks, including inequity in access, possible overreliance on technology, depersonalization, distraction, unclear evidence for some technologies, and ethical concerns around AI. They call for more research on long-term effects, specific student populations, assessment, teacher preparation, and the implications of generative AI for mathematics education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed narrative review, not an experimental or meta-analytic study. It synthesizes literature across multiple technology areas, but the paper itself does not provide a transparent systematic search protocol or causal estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad, plausible impacts on mathematics education practice and policy, especially around AI, blended learning, and inequality, but it reports no direct effect sizes or primary outcome data. Its influence is conceptual and field-synthesizing rather than demonstrably outcome-changing from new empirical evidence.

interventions.use_case: Narrative review of digital technology trends in mathematics education, including AI systems, hyper-personalisation, flipped/blended learning, online collaboration/social media, computer algebra systems, dynamic geometry, videos, AR/VR, and blockchain-related tools.

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes adjacent evidence rather than reporting a new empirical estimate. It argues that digital technologies can shift mathematics learning away from procedural calculation toward conceptual understanding and mathematical thinking, but also notes that some tools may accelerate problem solving without deepening understanding. No pooled effect size, sample size, or quantitative estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding, mathematical thinking, problem-solving, procedural fluency (as discussed across prior studies)

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, digital tools are described as potentially increasing engagement, motivation, and self-paced learning, especially in flipped and blended mathematics settings. The paper also flags risks of disengagement, depersonalization, distraction, and overreliance on technology, but does not provide a single study-level estimate.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, self-paced learning, persistence (as reported in cited studies)

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that technology-supported mathematics learning can foster collaboration, argumentation, critical thinking, and independent learning through social media, collaborative environments, and AI-supported personalization. At the same time, it warns that easy access to answers may reduce reflective thinking and that AI or informal platforms can undermine deeper problem solving if poorly used.
finding.measure: Collaboration, critical thinking, independent learning, argumentation, problem-solving (as discussed across cited studies)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that COVID-19, unequal home internet access, and the rise of AI are reshaping curriculum, assessment, and the role of home and community in mathematics education. It highlights both opportunity for broader participation and the risk that social inequality and access gaps will make education for all more difficult, but provides no quantitative effect estimate.
finding.measure: Curriculum, assessment, access/inequality, home environment, institutional change
